text: Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisementPsychologyWhy Forgive and Forget is Bad AdviceA conversation with MacArthur fellow Felipe de Brigard about how forgiveness reshapes the memory of atrocityKFBy Kristen French3:00 PM CDT on October 7, 2026Add Nautilus to GoogleForgiveness is a core virtue across religious traditions the world over, but the concept seems to present a paradox. Forgetting past hurts can feel potentially catastrophic, making us vulnerable to similar offenses in the future from the original perpetrator or from others like them. But letting go may bring us peace from feelings of resentment, anger or hate. The memories of these hurts can haunt people for a lifetime, often leading to repeated violence or perpetual war, some of the worst scourges of humankind.Duke University memory researcher, philosopher and cognitive scientist Felipe de Brigard has been studying the relationship between memory and forgiveness since the early 2000s with a grant from the John Templeton Foundation. He has just won a MacArthur Foundation grant to continue pursuing that work.Read more: “Are Some People Addicted to Revenge?”Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisement
